title: Sample-Efficient Kernel Mean Estimator with Marginalized Corrupted Data

problem.claim: Kernel mean estimation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space is important for kernel-based learning algorithms, and finite-sample estimation commonly uses an empirical average.

gap.claim: Existing work indicates that shrinkage can improve on the standard empirical-average estimator, motivating a different estimator for kernel mean estimation.

contributions.claim: The work proposes corrupting data examples with noise from known distributions and introduces the marginalized kernel mean estimator for kernel mean estimation under the corrupted distributions.
The work theoretically justifies that the marginalized kernel mean estimator introduces implicit regularization in kernel mean estimation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On a variety of tasks, the authors report that the marginalized kernel mean estimator is sample-efficient and achieves much lower estimation errors than existing estimators.

narrative_sequence.summary: Kernel mean estimation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space supports many kernel-based learning algorithms.
With finite samples, the empirical average is used as the standard kernel mean estimator.
Prior work shows that shrinkage methods can produce improved estimators.

The authors introduce a marginalized estimator based on known-distribution data corruption, justify its implicit regularization, and report sample-efficiency and lower estimation errors across varied tasks.

source_observation.claim: The estimator is constructed by marginalizing over noise from known distributions applied to data examples.

interpretation.claim: Known corruption can serve as an estimation mechanism that induces implicit regularization.

application.claim: Consider analytically marginalizing structured, known data perturbations when designing sample-efficient kernel mean estimators.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the approach applies when corruption distributions are unknown or misspecified.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the task types, datasets, baselines, sample sizes, or numerical estimation errors.
The abstract does not provide the theoretical assumptions, estimator formula, or proof details.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported empirical results.
